The European Union. A supranational political and economic union of twenty-seven member states, designed to prevent future European wars through economic integration and shared governance.

The origins trace back to 1951, when six nations—Belgium, France, West Germany, Italy, and the Netherlands—formed the European Coal and Steel Community. This agreement pooled coal and steel production under shared authority.

In 1957, the European Economic Community expanded integration to all economic sectors. By the nineteen-nineties, it was renamed the European Union and added political governance structures.

The EU operates through complex institutions: the European Commission as the executive, the Council of Ministers as the legislative body, and the European Parliament, which has been directly elected by citizens since 1979.

The Maastricht Treaty in 1992 introduced the euro, a shared currency adopted by nineteen EU member states. It symbolized continental unity but also created asymmetries between strong and weak economies.

Cold War membership divisions were profound. Western Europe joined the EU while Eastern Europe remained in the Soviet sphere until 1989. Post-Cold War expansion eastward after 2004 reshaped EU politics and enlarged the union significantly.

The 2008 financial crisis exposed structural vulnerabilities. Southern European nations like Greece, Spain, and Italy could not devalue currency to restore competitiveness, which triggered austerity and social upheaval.

Brexit in 2020 marked the first member departure, reflecting rising populism and doubt that EU membership served all citizens equally, particularly in economically depressed regions.

Contemporary EU debates center on climate policy, digital regulation, immigration quotas, and the balance between Brussels bureaucracy and national democracy.
